answer: This usually happens because self._text is no longer the same object instance that is actually inside the rendered layout (self._composite). Panel/Bokeh only pushes an update to the browser when a parameter changes on the exact widget object whose model is embedded in the document; if something elsewhere rebuilds self._composite (or creates a fresh StaticText) without updating self._text to match, mutating self._text.value silently changes an orphaned object that is not on screen anymore, so only a full page reload (which re-renders everything from scratch) shows it. Your workaround fixes this by cloning and reassigning both self._text and self._composite[0] to the same new object, resynchronizing them. Check whether any other method in your class rebuilds self._composite or reconstructs StaticText separately, and keep a single canonical reference. As a lighter alternative, try self._text.param.trigger('value') or wrapping the update in pn.io.hold()/pn.io.unlocked() to force a push, but the real fix is eliminating the reference desync rather than working around it every time.

Plaxis Output's Python API mainly exposes results for objects directly selectable in Output, and connection element results (rotation, moment) generally are not reachable via getsingleresult/getresult/tabulate the same way as ordinary structural elements, since connections report per node pair rather than as one result object. Try iterating the connection's underlying nodes instead of the connection itself, e.g. g_o.getresults(con.Nodes[0], phase, g_o.ResultTypes.Connection.Rotationtot, 'node'), or check g_o.ResultTypes.Connection for node-indexed variants. Also inspect g_o.Connections (or the phase's connection collection) for a results-capable subobject distinct from the definition objects in cons_NB. If none of the standard calls work, this looks like a real gap in the scripting API for "Connection information" data - worth checking the Bentley Plaxis Python API changelog for your specific version, or asking on the Plaxis support forum, since this data type may currently require reading manually from the Output GUI or an exported report rather than direct scripting. I cannot verify the exact call without your Plaxis version's API reference.

This means OPENAI_API_KEY is not actually set in the environment your Python process sees - os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY') is returning None, so the client refuses to start. Fixes: 1) Set it in the same shell before running the script: on PowerShell, $env:OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'; on macOS/Linux, export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'; then run the script from that same terminal session. 2) Or pass it directly: OpenAI(api_key='sk-...'), fine for quick testing but do not hardcode secrets in committed code. 3) If you use a .env file, it is NOT loaded automatically - install python-dotenv and call load_dotenv() before creating the client. 4) If running from an IDE (VS Code, PyCharm, Jupyter), setting the variable in a plain terminal will not affect the IDE's run configuration or kernel; set it in the IDE's own environment settings or restart the IDE/kernel after exporting it system-wide. Also double-check for typos in the variable name and that the key itself is valid and not revoked.

FlopCountAnalysis expects its second argument to be the actual inputs tuple matching the model's forward signature - you should not wrap the model in a plain function. Pass all positional arguments together: FlopCountAnalysis(model, (input_tensor, arg1, arg2)). Wrapping forward in a bare function like _wrapped_forward breaks it because fvcore's internals expect a real nn.Module (it likely walks named_modules() to attach per-module hooks, or traces it as a module), so handing it a plain function as the "model" raises an error (commonly an AttributeError). If some arguments must be fixed/keyword-only, write a thin nn.Module subclass whose forward hardcodes those extra args and calls the real model internally, then pass that module together with the remaining tensor inputs as a tuple to FlopCountAnalysis. In short: keep the real model object as the first argument, supply a tuple of every forward-required input as the second argument, and only wrap with a module (never a plain function) if you truly need to bind extra arguments.

Bash has no built-in multi-character split, but gawk's RS (record separator) accepts a literal string, so you can replicate str.split() and load the pieces into a Bash array with mapfile:
mapfile -t parts < <(awk -v RS='dab' '{print}' <<< "$text")
Each element of parts corresponds to one chunk between occurrences of 'dab', matching Python's list.split() output (including a leading empty/whitespace-only element if the text starts with the delimiter). This needs gawk specifically - mawk/POSIX awk do not support multi-character RS. If gawk is not available, fall back to substituting the delimiter with a NUL byte and reading with mapfile -d '':
mapfile -d '' -t parts < <(sed 's/dab/\x00/g' <<< "$text")
Either way you end up with a real Bash array (access via ${parts[@]}, ${parts[0]}, etc.) instead of just printed text, which is what you said you actually need for collecting into an array.

Sympy already has this built in - you do not need mpmath at all. Use sympy.rad(), which converts degrees to radians symbolically:
import sympy as sym
sym.rad(126)  # -> 7*pi/10
This returns an exact symbolic Rational*pi expression (auto-simplified), not a float. For Unicode/pretty rendering use sym.pprint(sym.rad(126)) or sym.latex(sym.rad(126)) in a notebook. There is also sym.deg() for the inverse conversion. If your installed sympy version genuinely lacks rad/deg (very old release), the manual equivalent is sym.pi*sym.Rational(126, 180), which sympy reduces the same way. No mpmath needed - mpmath.radians always returns an arbitrary-precision float, which is exactly why you got a numeric result instead of a symbolic one; sympy's own rad/deg functions are the symbolic equivalent you are looking for.

The bytes you show for the apostrophe (E2 80 99) are actually valid UTF-8 for U+2019, so that exact sequence should not trigger InvalidUtf8 - which suggests the real file on disk is not encoded the way your hex dump implies. A very common cause: the JSON was produced by something using Windows-1252/CP1252 (copy-pasted from Word/Excel, or saved by Notepad as "ANSI"), where the curly apostrophe is a single byte 0x92 - that lone byte is invalid as standalone UTF-8 and is exactly what Polars' strict UTF-8 JSON parser rejects. Verify the actual on-disk bytes (open the file in a hex editor, or in Python: open(path,'rb').read()) rather than trusting a retyped example. Fix by re-encoding the file to real UTF-8 before reading it, e.g. text = open('file.json', encoding='cp1252').read(); open('file_utf8.json','w',encoding='utf-8').write(text); df = pl.read_json('file_utf8.json'). Alternatively read+decode in Python's more permissive json module and build the frame with pl.DataFrame(json.loads(raw_bytes.decode('cp1252'))).

scikit-learn estimators require 2D X (n_samples, n_features) and, for multi-output, a 2D y (n_samples, n_outputs) - not 3D+ arrays. Flattening X into shape (n_samples, 6) is the right move; keep doing that. But your targets look like continuous coordinates, (34,24), (13,30), not discrete classes, so this is really a multi-output regression problem, not classification - which is why LogisticRegression gives near-random "accuracy": accuracy/precision/recall are the wrong metrics for continuous targets. Keep y two-dimensional instead of collapsing it to one number: y = np.array([[34,24],[13,30], ...]). Then use a regressor with native or wrapped multi-output support, e.g. sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression, RandomForestRegressor, or sklearn.multioutput.MultiOutputRegressor(SomeRegressor()) if the base estimator does not support multi-output directly. Evaluate with mean_squared_error/r2_score per output instead of accuracy. If (X,Y) are actually categorical bins rather than continuous measurements, use MultiOutputClassifier instead - but given the values shown, regression is almost certainly what you want.

pyhtml escapes any string you pass as a child, which is why the table shows up as literal markup text - that is expected safety behavior, not a bug. If raw()/Raw() does not exist in the version you have installed, check that version's source or changelog for the current name of its "unsafe/do-not-escape" node type - implementations vary and some rename it (e.g. Markup, NotEscaped, or a str subclass the renderer skips). As a fallback that works regardless of the library's exact API, render the skeleton with pyhtml normally, then splice the table HTML into the final string yourself instead of inside the DSL tree: build shell = h.html(h.head(h.title('Student Data')), h.body(h.h1('Student Details'), '__TABLE__')), then page = str(shell).replace('__TABLE__', sdf.to_html(index=False)). Or skip the DSL for that one node and assemble the final HTML with an f-string around sdf.to_html(index=False) directly. This guarantees the table is inserted unescaped without depending on whichever raw-HTML helper your specific pyhtml version happens to support.

The RAM sawtooth pattern (climbs to about 6.5GB, crashes, restarts on a new port, repeats) is Pylance's analysis process being OOM-killed and auto-restarting - it is crash-looping while indexing, not simply slow. The likely cause is Pylance trying to enumerate and analyze the huge ML site-packages tree (torch, unsloth, triton, flash-attn, CUDA libs) inside the container. Fixes: 1) Give WSL2 more memory via your .wslconfig file ([wsl2] section, memory=12GB or more) and restart WSL. 2) In .vscode/settings.json set 'python.analysis.diagnosticMode' to 'openFilesOnly' instead of workspace-wide. 3) Exclude heavy packages from analysis via 'python.analysis.exclude', e.g. '**/site-packages/torch/**' and '**/site-packages/triton/**'. 4) Add site-packages to 'files.watcherExclude' so the file watcher is not also overwhelmed. 5) Lower 'python.analysis.userFileIndexingLimit'. Also confirm Docker Desktop's resource limits (Settings > Resources) allow enough RAM/CPU, since WSL2 defaults to roughly half the host RAM, which may still be too little alongside VS Code, Pylance, and the container's own ML processes running at once.

At 5000x50x100x100 = 2.5 billion elements, a float64 output array alone is about 20GB, and your gaussian() creates several more full-size temporaries (x-mu, the division, the square, exp, another division) - that multiplies memory traffic several times over and is almost certainly your real bottleneck, not raw FLOPs. Quick wins: 1) Use float32 instead of float64 to halve memory bandwidth if precision allows. 2) Use numexpr, which evaluates the whole expression in one fused, multithreaded pass without materializing every intermediate: import numexpr as ne; ne.evaluate("exp(-0.5*((x-mu)/sigma)**2)/(sqrt(2*pi)*sigma)"). This alone often gives a large speedup on exactly this pattern. 3) Or write it with numba's @njit(parallel=True) and explicit loops to avoid temporaries entirely. 4) If a GPU is available, cupy is a near drop-in replacement for numpy and this embarrassingly parallel elementwise workload will run much faster on it. 5) Precompute 1/sqrt(2*pi) once. Also consider whether you need the full dense array at once, or can stream/chunk it to cut peak memory.

No framework or code is shown, so here is the general pattern: hook a function into your application's shutdown/close event rather than trying to detect it externally. If it is a plain script, register with atexit: atexit.register(make_graph) runs make_graph() on normal interpreter exit. If it is a GUI app (e.g. Tkinter), bind the window's close event instead, since atexit does not reliably fire on abrupt GUI termination: root.protocol('WM_DELETE_WINDOW', on_close), where on_close() builds the graph then destroys the window. Inside that handler: read the log with pandas.read_excel('log.xlsx'), plot with matplotlib (df.plot(...); plt.savefig('graph.png')) or plotly, then to "display it automatically" either open the saved image with the OS default viewer (os.startfile('graph.png') on Windows, subprocess.run(['open', path]) on macOS, xdg-open on Linux), or, if using plotly, call fig.show() which opens it directly in a browser tab. If your data-collection app already has its own exit hook or callback system, prefer that over atexit for reliability.

This is almost always a package-version mismatch between your local environment and the Azure Functions runtime - Azure Functions installs from requirements.txt into its own environment, which can resolve different SQLAlchemy/pyodbc/pandas versions than what you tested locally, and some combinations mishandle collation-bearing type objects when building parameterized INSERTs via to_sql/fast_executemany. Also, feeding inspector.get_columns()-derived types straight into dtype= is unusual: those are full reflected TypeEngine objects carrying a COLLATE clause meant for DDL, not parameter binding, and certain pyodbc/SQLAlchemy versions choke on that in an INSERT context ("not a string" means the driver received the type object itself, not a value). Try: 1) pin exact versions of pandas, sqlalchemy, and pyodbc in requirements.txt to match your local venv; 2) build a minimal dtype_mapping using plain types without collation, e.g. sqlalchemy.types.String(length=100), instead of the introspected column type; 3) confirm ODBC Driver 17 is actually installed in the Azure Functions worker, since local versus cloud driver availability commonly differs too.

Both statements are true, they just apply to different objects. Model.objects.all() called on a manager always returns a brand-new, unevaluated QuerySet - no caching involved yet. Calling .all() on an already-evaluated QuerySet instance (not the manager) clones it into a fresh QuerySet without carrying over the old result cache, so evaluating that clone re-hits the database - that is the "get updated results" behavior the first doc excerpt describes. The prefetch_related case is a deliberate special case: prefetching populates a private _prefetched_objects_cache on the related manager, and calling .all() on that specific related manager (e.g. restaurant.pizzas.all()) checks for that cache first and returns it directly instead of cloning and querying, so that calling .all() does not silently defeat the point of prefetching. So: plain .all() on an evaluated queryset = fresh clone = queries again on next evaluation; .all() on a prefetched relation's manager = intentionally cache-aware and skips the query. It is not inconsistent, just two different code paths with different rules.

This is almost always caused by PyInstaller building from a different Python environment than the one where numpy/plotly are actually installed (a global interpreter versus your conda/venv), or by numpy's binary extension modules and plotly's package data (JSON schema files under plotly/package_data) not being auto-detected by PyInstaller's static import analysis. Try building with explicit collection instead of manually editing datas/hiddenimports: pyinstaller --onefile --collect-all numpy --collect-all plotly main.py. In the .spec file this is hiddenimports += collect_submodules('plotly') + collect_submodules('numpy') and datas += collect_data_files('plotly'), imported from PyInstaller.utils.hooks. Also delete the build/ and dist/ folders and the old main.spec before rebuilding so stale caches do not mask the fix, and double check which python/pip PyInstaller itself is invoked from (where pyinstaller, and pip show numpy in that exact shell) to rule out an environment mismatch - that is the single most common cause of a "numpy not installed" error in a build that otherwise runs fine from source.

What you already have - a Python list containing 9 numpy arrays - genuinely is a "list of lists" in the sense you mean; the only difference from what you expected is how it prints. A list of 9 separate arrays reprs as [array([...]), array([...]), ...] with each array's own brackets, whereas a single 2D array reprs as one block [[...] [...] ...]. To get that combined double-bracket look, turn it into one real 2D array:
rows = [np.arange(0, 25.05, 0.05) for _ in range(9)]
arr2d = np.array(rows)
# or directly:
arr2d = np.tile(np.arange(0, 25.05, 0.05), (9, 1))
Avoid [np.arange(...)] * 9 style repetition if you ever mutate a row later - that repeats the same underlying array by reference 9 times (not an issue for read-only use, but worth knowing). np.tile is the most direct one-liner for "repeat this exact row N times" as a proper 2D array.

Cancellation only takes effect at an await suspension point. Your for loop over source never awaits, so the task never yields back to the event loop - the cancellation request has nowhere to be delivered until the loop finishes, and if source is effectively infinite it also likely starves your asyncio.sleep(3) in main from ever getting to run concurrently in the first place. Fix by adding an await checkpoint inside the loop:
for item in source:
    print("Working")
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
That yields control each iteration and is where CancelledError actually gets raised once cancel() is called. Your existing except Exception will not swallow it - CancelledError is a BaseException subclass since Python 3.8, so it still propagates to your finally block as written. If source is a blocking/CPU-bound generator that genuinely cannot await anything, run it in a thread via loop.run_in_executor and signal cancellation with a threading.Event instead, since real OS-thread work cannot be interrupted by asyncio.Task.cancel().

The question text is cut off before showing the actual IllegalArgumentException message, so this is a best-effort guess: transformWithStateInPandas value-state schemas with nested ArrayType columns inside a StructType are a known pain point with the default UnsafeRow-based state store encoding - some versions raise IllegalArgumentException because that encoding does not fully support certain nested array/collection layouts. If your Spark version supports it, try switching to Avro-based state encoding before defining the state: spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.encodingFormat", "avro"). Also confirm your Spark version actually supports ArrayType-typed columns inside getValueState's StructType - this API changed significantly across the 3.5/4.0 release line - and that RocksDBStateStoreProvider plus the arbitrary-state-API configs are mutually compatible versions. If it persists, try flattening state to parallel scalar/StringType-encoded fields (e.g. comma-joined strings) instead of true ArrayType columns as a workaround, since scalar state types are far more robustly supported across versions than nested array state currently is.

The question text cuts off right before showing the actual error message, so I cannot diagnose the exact exception - but the most common failure with this pattern is NoSuchElementException on match.find_element(by='xpath', value='./td[1]') for header rows: driver.find_elements(by='xpath', value='//tr') grabs every <tr>, including the <thead> row, which holds <th> cells rather than <td>, so the very first iteration throws. Fix by skipping the header, e.g. iterate matches[1:], or scope the xpath to body rows only, //tbody/tr. Other likely culprits with this exact code: the click on all_matches_button may fire before the table finishes loading, so find_elements('//tr') returns an incomplete set - add an explicit wait such as WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.presence_of_all_elements_located(...)) right after the click; and a cookie-consent overlay could make the initial click raise ElementClickInterceptedException. Wrapping each row's extraction in try/except and adding explicit waits after driver.get() and after the button click resolves most variants of this.

There is no built-in one-liner to make an existing @dataclass's fields all Optional without touching each annotation, because @dataclass generates __init__ at class-definition time directly from the annotations and defaults present. The practical fix that avoids rewriting 30 fields is to not change the class at all - instead merge a full None-defaults dict with your possibly-partial incoming data before constructing:
import dataclasses
defaults = {f.name: None for f in dataclasses.fields(User)}
user = User(**{**defaults, **attributes})
This makes any missing key default to None no matter how many fields you add later, with zero changes to User itself. If you want it enforced on the class, write a small decorator that runs after @dataclass and rebuilds __init__, or switch to pydantic's BaseModel, where Optional[...] = None per field is still explicit but partial construction and validation are more first-class. There is no "all_optional=True" flag on the standard library dataclass decorator itself.
